title: The Talmud Page: These and These
hookLine: Hasidic, Lithuanian, Sephardi, modern and women's voices, all in one conversation
carry: the talmud keeps both sides: these and these
tomorrow: Moses sat in a class and couldn't follow it. why was he comforted?

lines: ONE BIG PAGE ON THE TABLE.
cards: A kitchen table, cleared after dinner. An old man unfolds one large printed page and smooths it flat with both hands. His granddaughter leans in, expecting a paragraph.

Instead there's a block of text in the middle, and around it, in smaller type, more text, and around that, more again, like a group chat where everyone is replying to everyone, except some of them lived centuries apart.
She asks the obvious thing: who's talking? He taps the middle, then the edges. Everyone, he says.

teach.b: That's a page of Talmud, and it's built like a conversation. In the center sits the Mishnah, and the Gemara, the sages' long discussion of it. On the inside margin, Rashi, the great commentator, explaining word by word.

On the outside, the Tosafot, a circle of later scholars arguing with Rashi and with each other. Then more notes, from more generations, pressed in at the edges. Nobody cleared the table before the next voice sat down.
And here is the detail to tell a friend: the losing opinions stay on the page.
The Mishnah itself asks why it records a minority view if the law follows the majority, and answers, so that a later court could lean on it someday.
The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice settling a long dispute between two schools: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. Both sides kept.

teach.h: THIS PATH'S VOICES, ON ONE PAGE.
teach.b: Now look back at the voices of these weeks and see them on that page. Rebbe Nachman finding the good point. Rabbi Soloveitchik, from a Lithuanian line of learning, bringing holiness into the details.
Nechama Leibowitz asking for the real question. Rabbi Ovadia Yosef restoring Sephardi custom. Heschel's wonder, Buber's you.
Henrietta Szold saying Kaddish herself, and a woman's tkhine in three languages. They didn't always agree, and some would have argued hard across the table. That's not a flaw in the tradition.
One long conversation, still going, with a seat left open at the edge.

how: In a study hall, pairs read a page of Talmud aloud, moving from the center text to Rashi and the Tosafot in the margins; the page layout itself keeps commentators from different centuries side by side.

o: a single sage's book of rulings, written alone
the Talmud page: every generation's voice kept together
a phone call that runs on for hours with a friend

games.q: who sits where on the page — tap the pairs.
p: kept, so a later court can use it

s: the Talmud only records the opinion that won
the losing views stay on the page; the Mishnah says why: a later court might lean on them.
the Talmud says both schools' words are the words of the living God
these and these, it says, and the law follows the house of Hillel.
the commentaries in the margins all agree with the center
the Tosafot argue with Rashi and with each other. it's a conversation, not a chorus.

games.q: your family's group chat splits over where to hold the reunion, and your uncle wants to delete the losing side's messages to 'keep it clean.' what does the Talmud page suggest?
o: keep them: a losing view can matter later, and everyone stays at the table.
delete them: once a decision's made, the old arguments only cause trouble.
start a new chat with only the side that won, so it feels settled.
games.why: the Mishnah keeps minority views so a later court can lean on them, and the Talmud calls both schools the words of the living God. both sides kept.

practice: Count on your fingers the voices from these weeks that stayed with you: a philosopher, a poet, a rabbi, a woman who said Kaddish herself. Let each one get a finger and a moment of thanks.
Then settle on one, your favorite so far, and hold that name for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: One long conversation: the Talmud page, with every generation's voice around the center, the losing views kept.

orig.note: Hebrew: these and these. From Eruvin 13b: these and these are the words of the living God.

carryVoice: Your line: the Talmud keeps both sides, these and these. Every voice kept, even the ones who lost. That's day one thousand six hundred forty-six.
